blocks.source: Vol III, The Foundation Model, § Historical Perspective and Further Reading
blocks.md: The foundation model call joins two intellectual lineages that developed independently for decades. The first is statistical language modeling. @shannon1948 framed natural language as a discrete stochastic process, treating English as a sequence of symbols drawn from conditional probability distributions and generating text from successively longer context windows. @bengio2003neural replaced high-dimensional count tables with a continuous neural function over distributed word representations, establishing the autoregressive next-token factorization that modern architectures still use. The Transformer made that formulation parallelizable across token positions during training.

questions.q: The section **Historical Perspective and Further Reading** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Likelihood is not truth, schema conformance is not permission, a passing test covers only exercised behavior, and self-review re-samples the same distribution, so each gate is chosen for the one property it certifies and a fallible checker leaves a residual defect share given by Bayes.

A per-state logit mask guarantees a completed output is in the enforced language, but only for syntax, only on COMPLETED status, and an over-constrained schema forces confabulation unless it offers an explicit unknown variant.

Prefill is bounded by arithmetic and unbatched decode by weight bandwidth, so one output token costs roughly as much time as several hundred prompt tokens and output length is the primary latency lever.

Reduction order and serving-path changes flip contested argmax choices even at temperature zero, so the runtime logs model revision, serving configuration, and sampling settings with every call and replays recorded responses when behavior must be reproduced.
